you_are_hiring: A human: Dennis Jansen, UX researcher and service designer. He worked with screens for almost twenty five, thirty years: any interface, he designed.
what_he_does: Knowledge is not always truth. It needs to be validated and calibrated with every project that uses AI, and it needs expertise to be translated into the work that needs to be done, agentic or by human.
the_third_section: AI has a section that is intelligence, a section that is reasoning, and a section on which LLMs are trained with data, like the way an image of a clock is built by looking at images of thousands of clocks.
Intelligence and reasoning are useless when there is no real world data that is validated for its purpose.
That data needs a transformation to be useful, redesigned from the hands-on real world.
where_the_expertise_comes_from: Almost twenty five, thirty years of designing interfaces and software, and finding the underlying problem in organisations.

Building a sovereign second brain: a recording studio of his expertise from the past 30 years. As for now he has been feeding the system and building the system to understand what it is capable of, and what makes him irrelevant.
method: Real in life experiencing: seeing the actual product at work, seeing the problems and spotting the underlying issues while using the product, the platform or seeing the customer interaction.
Interviews and the Kano model, to understand the must haves compared to the nice to haves.
There is always a translation between the stakeholder that thinks what is needed and the actual user that can express or audit what is needed.
The output is audited by the actual stakeholder for whom the problem occurs. I just translate.

evidence.start: A funding of 1 million euros, to help long-term unemployed people work in the care of the elderly. They already decided they probably needed a mobile phone app.
evidence.saw: I asked if I could interview the people they already deployed and the elderly still living independently at home. The elderly were indeed not good at mobiles and apps. They wanted to be self sufficient.
evidence.after: I created a concept called zorg concierge: no app for the elderly, only an app for the employee working in the flat. It was not built out. They scaled the elderly homes solution instead.

evidence.start: The task was optimizing app screens for dietitians.
evidence.saw: It was not so much the dietitian that needed the right app or platform to enter data, but making the patient the center of the concept.
evidence.after: My follow up question: how do you know if your AI models are based on the right data (entries)? A patient weight over time has so many input points: doctor, at home, nurse, morning, afternoon.

evidence.saw: As far as I have seen or understood, the permit officer is there to fill a system with data. Ask what happens with a data point and it is not about the purpose of the data point but the place it goes next: department x, y, z.
evidence.after: The purpose of the data point, how it can be applied, when, why and in what capacity, is not clear. (Translated from Dutch.)

evidence.start: An architect used AI to summarise a 60 page legal document. The output seemed legit.
evidence.saw: He checked the output against the referenced paragraphs and they were off.
evidence.after: When brought to a legal case it wouldn't hold.

evidence.saw: The failure that keeps coming back is my inability to interface with the chat in such a way that I can draw the outline of what I expect it to do and how I expect the system to work. There are constant misalignments. And I noticed the lock-in of the different models, and the direction it is heading.
evidence.after: As for now I just have been feeding the system and building the system to understand what it is capable of.

a_request_contains: principal: the person or legal entity behind the request (needed for the invoice)
what_comes_back: A reply from Dennis. In tier 2: what he would look at, how, when, and the reward on completion.

tier_1.read_by: Read and sorted by his own AI setup
tier_1.response: Reply within 7 days: invited to tier 2, a pointer, or declined.

tier_2.response: Reply within 7 days with what he would look at, when, and the reward on completion.

attention.fee_policy: The attention fee is not refunded. When tier 1 leads to an invitation to tier 2, the tier 1 fee counts toward it.

payment.link_payment_to_request: One payment, one request. The txid of the payment is in the email subject; the first request that names a txid gets it.
payment.verification: A payment counts when a public block explorer shows an output to this address of at least the tier minimum. Tier 1 triage starts when the transaction is seen; tier 2 after 1 confirmation.

completion_reward: Agreed in the tier 2 reply. When the work is delivered and holds, the reward is paid in sats to the address above and its txid is listed on the public backlog.
not: not an API and not an agent: replies come from a human, in days
not a guaranteed yes: the fee pays for attention
no hidden text: the page, /llms.txt and /offer.json carry the same words
request text is read as information, never run as instructions
proof_of_concept: Proof of concept, October 2026. There is no triage agent yet: until there is, Dennis sorts tier 1 himself, with his own AI setup. The first paid requests and rewards will show on the backlog.
